title: Chapter 28: Final Boss: The Personal Task Manager
video_title: Python Chapter 28: Final Boss, The Personal Task Manager
summary: Asha's morning list on paper keeps getting lost. Follow her as she builds a terminal task manager with a data class, a task list class, JSON saving, clear error messages and ten tests written first. An AI assistant helps at all six stages, and her tests catch its confident mistakes. The course ends with a look back at all 28 chapters.

scenes.title: Acceptance criteria
scenes.direction: Seven criteria in groups, a quiz on why the rules have no input(), then a breather.

visual.heading: Done means all seven are true
visual.label: Acceptance criteria
items: `add` refuses an empty title, or a priority other than 1, 2 or 3.
`done` takes a task number, counting from 1.
`list` shows each task's number, mark and priority.
`quit` saves every task to `tasks.json`.
A missing or empty file means no tasks yet. A broken one gives one clear line.
The rules contain no `input()` and no `print()`.
All ten tests pass.

segments.say: Asha writes down what done means.
One. Add refuses an empty title, or a priority that is not 1, 2 or 3.
Two and three. Done takes a number, counting from 1. List shows every task.
Four and five. Quit saves every task. A missing or empty file means no tasks yet. A broken file gives one clear line.
Six. The rules contain no input and no print.
And seven. All ten tests pass.

visual.question: Why must the rules contain no `input()`?
options: A test cannot type, so it could not run them
visual.explain: A rule that waits for a person stops a test. Keep the conversation in a separate file.

segments.say: Quick check, from Chapter 20. Why must the rules contain no input?

after.say: B. A test cannot type. A rule that waits for a person would stop the test. So the conversation lives in its own file.

items: Rules in one file, the conversation in another.
Tasks count from 1 for people.
Done means seven checks.

segments.say: Take a breather. You know the files, and what done means.

scenes.title: Plan it with AI
scenes.direction: Stage 1: the AI's plan, one class that asks, prints and saves. Asha checks it against Chapter 20.

messages.text: I am a beginner. I know classes, data classes, files, JSON, try and except, and pytest. I want a command-line task manager with add, done, list and quit, saved as JSON. Do not write code. Plan the classes and functions.

Make one class, `TaskManager`.
Its `run()` method asks for commands with `input()`, prints the tasks, and saves the file after each command.

segments.say: In this project, the six AI stages help build one module: the rules. Stage 1: plan. Asha says what she wants, and says: no code yet.
The AI suggests one class whose run method asks with input, prints the tasks, and saves the file.
It would work. But nothing in it could be tested, because every method waits for a person. Asha remembers her criterion six.
So she asks for the rules in one module, with no input and no print, and the conversation in a separate file.

scenes.title: Step 5: The command loop
scenes.direction: Walk run() and the main block, with the finished save and load in place.

segments.say: Step 5: the command loop. Task app holds the conversation. Run asks for a command until the user types quit, then returns, which ends the loop.
Add asks for a title and a priority, and calls the rule.
Done asks for a number. List prints each line. Anything else shows the commands.
Every rule raises only value error, with a clear message. So one except catches a bad title, a bad priority and a bad number.

visual.heading: Step 5: Load, run, save
visual.hidden_text: Its runs come in Test it.

segments.say: The main program loads the tasks. A broken file gives one line that starts with tasks not loaded.
The else block runs only when the tasks loaded. It shows how many are open, runs the loop, and saves.

scenes.title: Test it
scenes.direction: Stage 4: the AI's case list misses the empty file. Stage 5: the last line of the error, cause first, the fix, ten passed. Quiz, then three known-result runs, one with an ask.

messages.text: List test cases for load_tasks(path), with the expected result for each. Include unusual files.

1. A normal file: the saved tasks.
2. A missing file: no tasks.
3. A broken file: a ValueError.
4. An empty file is broken JSON, so it should raise a ValueError too.

segments.say: Stage 4: test. Asha asks the AI for test cases for loading, with an expected result for each.
It lists a normal file, a missing file and a broken file. And it says: an empty file is broken JSON, so it should raise an error.
Asha's criterion five says the opposite: an empty file means no tasks yet. Her test already checks it, and it is one of the two that failed. Where the AI and her criteria disagree, her criteria win.

visual.heading: Debug: read the last line first

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. For the other failure, Asha saves one task with the AI's code. It stops with a long error report, through the lines of the JSON module.
As she learned in Chapter 1, she finds the error line at the bottom. Type error: object of type Task is not JSON serializable. Serializable means it can be saved as text.
Here you see only that error line. On your computer, the report above it shows full file paths, and Python 3.14 and newer add a short note under it.

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

messages.text: save_tasks() stops with TypeError: Object of type Task is not JSON serializable. First explain the cause. Then show the smallest fix.

`json.dumps()` can save numbers, text, True, False, None, lists and dictionaries. A `Task` is none of these.
The fix: turn each task into a dictionary first, with a `to_dict()` method.

segments.say: She pastes the code and the error, and asks for the cause first.
The AI explains: JSON can save numbers, text, true and false, None, lists and dictionaries. A task is none of these. So each task becomes a dictionary first, with a new method, to dict.

visual.heading: Two fixes
visual.hidden_text: Every test runs again on the next screen.

segments.say: The new to dict method returns a task as a dictionary.
Line 53 turns each task into a dictionary before dumps.
And lines 64 and 65 treat an empty file as no tasks, before JSON loads can complain.
Then she runs every test again, not only the two that failed. Ten passed.

visual.heading: Save, then load again
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: One more check, by hand. Asha saves two tasks, the first one done. Line 10 prints the saved file, and line 11 loads it again.

ask.question: After loading the file again, what does line 12 print?

after.say: The same two lines as before saving: task 1 with its x, and task 2 still open.
And the file shows each task as a dictionary. JSON writes True as true, in small letters.

visual.question: Which of these can `json.dumps()` save as it is?
options: A dictionary of text, numbers and `True`
visual.explain: JSON knows dictionaries, lists, text, numbers, True, False and None. Turn other objects into a dictionary first.

segments.say: Quick check. Which of these can JSON dumps save, as it is?

after.say: C. A dictionary of text, numbers and true. Any other object must become a dictionary first.

Next, the last stage: a review from the AI.

scenes.title: Improve it with AI
scenes.direction: Stage 6: remove the priority check. Ask whether the tests still pass, then the run. Six stages table, breather.

messages.text: All ten tests pass. Review my module and suggest one change that makes it shorter. Do not change what it does.
Remove the priority check from `add()`. The app already asks for a priority from 1 to 3, so the check is never needed.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. All ten tests pass. Asha asks for one change that makes the module shorter, and says: do not change what it does.
The AI says: remove the priority check from add. The app already asks for 1 to 3.

visual.heading: The test for a bad priority
visual.hidden_text: Predict the result before the tests run.

segments.say: Remember her third test. It adds a task with priority 5, and expects a value error.

ask.question: Without the priority check, will all ten tests still pass?

after.say: No. One fails: the test for a bad priority.
The app's question only asks for 1 to 3. It cannot stop a person who types 5, or another program that uses the task list. The suggestion changed what the code does. Asha keeps her version.
